transcript:
[Doctor]: Good morning, Mr. Diaz. How are you feeling today?

[Patient]: Good morning, doctor. I feel very tired and short of breath.

[Doctor]: Hmm, I see. Can you tell me more about when these symptoms started?

[Patient]: It’s been getting worse over the past two months. I feel tired all the time, and I get short of breath even when I’m just walking a short distance.

[Doctor]: I’m sorry to hear that. Have you noticed any changes in your urine output?

[Patient]: Yes, I’m not going to the bathroom as much as I used to. It’s less frequent and less in amount.

[Doctor]: Hmm, have you experienced any nausea or vomiting?

[Patient]: I do feel nauseous sometimes, but I haven’t vomited.

[Doctor]: Have these symptoms affected your daily activities?

[Patient]: Yes, very much. I need a lot of help from my family to do basic things now.

[Doctor]: I understand. Let’s go through your medical history. You have a history of hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus, correct?

[Patient]: Yes, that’s correct.

[Doctor]: Are you following the dietary recommendations given to you?

[Patient]: I try, but I still eat a lot of salty and processed foods.

[Doctor]: It’s important to follow a low-sodium diet. We’ll have a dietitian talk to you about that. Do you have any other symptoms like fever, chest pain, or dizziness?

[Patient]: No fever or chest pain. I don’t feel dizzy either.

[Doctor]: Any headaches?

[Patient]: No, no headaches.

[Doctor]: How about joint pain or muscle cramps?

[Patient]: No joint pain or muscle cramps.

[Doctor]: Any rashes or skin changes?

[Patient]: No, but my legs are swollen.

[Doctor]: I see. Let’s go over your vital signs. Your blood pressure today is 160/100 mmHg, your heart rate is 85 bpm, respiratory rate is 18 breaths per minute, temperature is 98.6°F, and oxygen saturation is 95% on room air.

[Patient]: Oh, okay.

[Doctor]: On your physical exam, I noticed a systolic murmur in your heart, diminished breath sounds at the bases of your lungs, and noticeable renal enlargement on palpation. You also have 2+ pitting edema in both lower limbs and delayed capillary refill.

[Patient]: What does that mean?

[Doctor]: It indicates that your kidneys are not functioning well, which is causing fluid retention. We are waiting for the results of your blood tests and a Doppler ultrasound to understand more about your kidney function and blood flow.

[Patient]: Okay, doctor.

[Doctor]: Based on your symptoms and history, we suspect hypertensive chronic kidney disease, possibly stage 4. You also have anemia likely due to chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and type 2 diabetes mellitus.

[Patient]: That sounds serious.

[Doctor]: It is, but we can manage it with the right treatment and lifestyle changes. We’ll start you on Enalapril 10 mg twice daily to help control your blood pressure. You’ll continue Atorvastatin 20 mg once daily for your cholesterol.

[Patient]: Will this help me feel better?

[Doctor]: Yes, it should help improve your symptoms over time. We’ll also start you on Erythropoietin injections to manage your anemia. It’s called Procrit, and you’ll take it once a week.

[Patient]: How will that help?

[Doctor]: It will help increase your red blood cell count, which should improve your energy levels and reduce fatigue.

[Patient]: Thank you, doctor.

[Doctor]: You’re welcome. We’ll also do some blood work, including a Comprehensive Metabolic Panel (CMP), Complete Blood Count (CBC), Vitamin D levels, and a Urinalysis. The Doppler Ultrasound will help us assess your renal blood flow and check for any structural anomalies.

[Patient]: What happens next?

[Doctor]: We’ll schedule a follow-up in two weeks to review your lab and imaging results and adjust your treatment if necessary. We’ll also refer you to a vascular surgeon to evaluate the possibility of creating an arteriovenous fistula for future dialysis access.

[Patient]: What is that?

[Doctor]: It’s a procedure to create a connection between an artery and a vein, which can be used for dialysis if needed.

[Patient]: I see.

[Doctor]: We’ll also have a dietary consultation to help you reduce your sodium intake and follow a renal-friendly diet. It’s important to stop smoking and reduce alcohol consumption if you do those. We’ll discuss ways to increase your physical activity within your limitations.

[Patient]: I’ll try my best.

[Doctor]: Great. We’ll provide educational materials in Spanish to ensure you understand your condition and treatment plan. We’ll also use medical interpreter services for future visits to ensure effective communication.

[Patient]: Thank you, doctor.

[Doctor]: You’re welcome. We’ll explore local community healthcare resources that may provide additional support and care for you.

[Patient]: That’s good to know.

[Doctor]: We’ll also monitor your blood pressure at home. Please keep a log and bring it to your follow-up appointments. It’s also important to closely monitor your blood sugar levels due to your diabetes.

[Patient]: Okay, I’ll do that.

[Doctor]: Do you have any questions for me?

[Patient]: No, I think I understand everything. Thank you for explaining it to me.

[Doctor]: You’re welcome. Remember, it’s important to adhere to your medications, follow the lifestyle modifications, and keep your follow-up appointments to manage your chronic conditions effectively.

[Patient]: I will, doctor. Thank you.

[Doctor]: Take care, Mr. Diaz. See you in two weeks.

[Patient]: Goodbye, doctor.
